title: Jane Eyre
synopsis: Gateshead, Lowood, Thornfield. You are small and plain and on fire on the inside. The master of the house has, you'll learn, a wife in the attic.

nodes.text: You have taken the breakfast-room curtain, the window seat behind it, and the volume of Bewick with the wrecks and the arctic rock in it. Rain drives across the shrubbery. John Reed finds you, explains that the books are his because the house is his, and throws one at your head. You bleed above the ear. Then you say aloud a thing you have never said, and the house comes down on you.

choices.consequence: You call him a wicked cruel boy, like a murderer, and mean the whole of it. Three servants carry you upstairs. Your aunt says nothing to him at all.
You hold still and let it land and make no sound, and the words stay lodged in your chest all evening like something swallowed the wrong way.

nodes.text: They put you in the room where your uncle died: the mahogany bed, the drawn blinds, the white counterpane, the easy chair standing pale as a throne. Nobody sleeps here. You are instructed to consider your ingratitude. In the dark glass over the chest, a small strange figure looks back at you. A light slides along the wall. You scream until there is no voice left, and they turn the key harder.

choices.consequence: You beat on the door and beg, and hear your aunt refuse from the other side of it. Something goes out of you that never entirely comes back.
You faint instead, which is afterward described downstairs as a fit of temper. You wake with the apothecary's fingers on your wrist and a bitterness you keep.

nodes.text: He is a black pillar with a face at the top of it and he asks whether you know where the wicked go after death. You say hell. He asks what you must do to avoid it. You say keep in good health and not die. Then your aunt tells him, in front of you, that you are a liar, and he agrees to take you and to have the school watch you for it.

choices.consequence: You look up the whole length of him without blinking. Afterward you tell your aunt to her face that you will never call her aunt again as long as you live.
You study the carpet pattern while a stranger is told you are deceitful. The word travels ahead of you to Lowood and is waiting when you arrive.

nodes.text: Eighty girls, one fire, and burnt porridge you cannot eat and are not permitted to leave. Your hair is cut off because curls are vanity. Brocklehurst's own daughters come to inspect you in velvet and ostrich feathers. He stands you on a stool for half an hour and names you a liar to the whole schoolroom. Helen Burns passes below and lifts her eyes to yours as she goes.

choices.consequence: She tells you to endure what you cannot cure. You argue with her about it for a year, lose every time, and love her without reservation.
You keep to the corner by the cold grate and learn French out of pure spite. Miss Temple sends for you at last and asks to hear your side.

nodes.text: Typhus takes half the school that spring and the garden fills with girls too weak to be indoors. Helen has not got typhus; it is her lungs, and everyone knows, and nobody tells you. You get up the stairs after midnight and into her bed. She says she is very happy and that you must not grieve for her. In the morning they carry you out asleep, and she is cold.

choices.consequence: You put your arms round her and she lets you, and you argue about heaven in whispers until she stops answering and you go on holding on.
You sit up beside her keeping watch, because sleeping seems like a desertion, and you lose to it anyway somewhere around three o'clock.

nodes.text: An inquiry follows the fever: fresh food, a better site, subscriptions from ashamed gentlemen, and Brocklehurst put under a committee that outvotes him. You stay eight years, six as a pupil and two as a teacher, and you are good at it. Then Miss Temple marries and goes, and the place is only a building again. You want liberty. You settle for a new servitude and write four lines for the county paper.

choices.consequence: You post it, then lie awake doing arithmetic on a governess's salary. The answer comes inside a week from a housekeeper at a place called Thornfield.
You give it one more term, and the term is very long, and the walls of that schoolroom have never fitted so exactly to the shape of your life.

nodes.text: A grey house with battlements, three storeys, rooks in the elms. Mrs. Fairfax turns out to be the housekeeper rather than the mistress, and is kind and a little deaf. Your pupil is a French child of seven who wants to sing about love and be told her sash is pretty. On the third floor, where nobody has business, someone laughs: low, distinct, and entirely without amusement in it.

choices.consequence: You ask, and are told it is Grace Poole, who sews upstairs. You accept the answer, and you begin quietly counting the times it happens.
You decide old houses make noises and go down to dinner. That night you stand a good while at the foot of the attic stairs, holding your candle low.

nodes.text: You walk to Hay to post a letter because you cannot bear another hour of the stillness. Hard frost, no wind, the moon coming up over the causeway. A dog goes past, then a horse and rider at speed, then a noise of ice and a man on the ground swearing with real thoroughness. He is heavy, dark-browed, not yet forty, and furious at needing anybody's shoulder.

choices.consequence: You offer your shoulder and he leans on it hard. Neither of you says one civil word, and you walk home afterward feeling oddly, unaccountably awake.
You wait until he is remounted, then go on and post your letter. Coming back you look at the lit windows of the house and are not glad to see them.

nodes.text: He sends for you after dinner, does not stand, tells you to sit, and looks at you a long moment before speaking. He asks whether you think him handsome. You say no. He wants to know if you were waiting for your people in the wood to bewitch his horse. He is your employer, he pays your salary, and he plainly wants, for reasons of his own, to be spoken to like a man.

choices.consequence: You answer in the smallest correct sentences available. He grows visibly bored, and you discover that you cannot bear to bore him.

choices.text: Hold your tongue except when honest
choices.consequence: You contradict him twice before the fire has burned down. He laughs like a man who has not had occasion to laugh in a considerable while.

nodes.text: Something wakes you: a laugh at your keyhole, a door somewhere, then smoke. His bed curtains are alight and he is asleep in the middle of it. You empty the basin over him and then the ewer, and he comes up cursing in a flooded bed. He goes upstairs. He comes back changed, tells you to say nothing to anybody, and takes both your hands and does not let go of them.

choices.consequence: You drag him clear and beat the flames out with his own scorched curtain. Your palms blister. He thanks you at three in the morning, in the dark, at length.
You shout once and then do it yourself, because nobody is coming down from the third floor, and you understand that before he ever explains it.

nodes.text: He has filled the house with visitors, among them Blanche Ingram, who is tall and handsome and discusses governesses as a category within your hearing. A fortune-teller arrives at the drawing room and asks specifically for the young person in the plain dress. She sits hunched over the fire under a bonnet and a red cloak and knows far too much, and the hands on the fire-screen are not an old woman's hands.

choices.consequence: You answer her questions truthfully, since truth costs you nothing, and watch the disguise get steadily less careful as each answer lands.
You say his name flatly and the bonnet comes off. He wanted to know what you thought of him. Now he does, and he is not pleased with it.

nodes.text: A cry in the night from directly above your ceiling, then a struggle, then a voice calling for help. He tells the assembled guests it was a servant's nightmare and sends them all back to bed in their dressing gowns. Then he takes you up to a room you have never seen and leaves you two hours with a bleeding stranger, a basin, a sponge, and instructions not to speak to him.

choices.consequence: You hold the sponge to a shoulder that has been bitten rather than cut, and listen to something moving behind the inner door until it is light.
You ask one question and the man begins to answer, and you stop him yourself, because you were told not to, and obedience is a habit you have kept.

nodes.text: Midsummer in the orchard after sundown, the fruit trees heavy, a nightingale somewhere down by the wall. He tells you he is marrying Miss Ingram and that you must go to Ireland, and repeats it until you break and tell him you have as much soul as he has, and heart, and that you are not a machine. Then he takes all of it back and asks you. In the night lightning splits the chestnut in two.

choices.consequence: You say yes, and the rain comes down as though the sky disagreed. You lie awake afterward making a list of the things you have not been told.
You ask three times whether he means it. Each answer is warmer than the last, and not one of them answers the question you did not know how to ask.

nodes.text: Two men are standing at the back of the church and one of them says the word impediment. There is a wife. She has been at Thornfield fifteen years behind Grace Poole's door on the third floor. He marches the whole wedding party up to see her: a figure that paces on all fours, then rises and goes for his throat. He binds her to a chair. Then he asks the room to look at her, and then at you.

choices.consequence: You go to your room, take off the veil, fold it, and sit down. Nobody has to convince you of anything. You already know what you are going to do.
You listen to him offer you the south of France, a white villa, and a name that would not be yours, and you want it, and that is the worst hour of your life.

nodes.text: You leave at four in the morning by the side door with twenty shillings and a parcel, past his room, where you can hear him walking up and down. He has offered you everything except a lawful name. You leave the pearl necklace on the dressing table where he put it. A coach takes you as far as the money reaches and sets you down at a crossroads where there is nothing but heather.

choices.consequence: You sleep in the heather with your face against the ground and beg bread at a farmhouse door, and you do not once turn back toward Millcote.
You give yourself until first light, sitting on the stairs with your boots already on, listening to a grown man weep in a room you have promised not to enter.

nodes.text: Three days of rain and no food, and you fall against a door on a hillside with a lit window. The servant sends you off; the young master, coming up the path behind you, looks at your face and lets you in. Diana and Mary give you bread and milk and do not ask your name until you can sit up. St. John gives you nothing warmer than his attention, which is extremely thorough.

choices.consequence: You spend a month getting your strength back among sisters who lend you books and laugh at their brother, and you very nearly forget to be watchful.
You ask for work the first morning you can stand, because taking what you cannot repay feels worse to you than three nights on the moor did.

nodes.text: Twenty village girls in a stone room, most unable to read, several not clean, none of them anybody's idea of important. You take a cottage with four whitewashed walls and a floor of sand. You teach them their letters, the names of the counties, and how to hem. Some evenings you sit with your hands flat in your lap and think about a house with battlements and rooks in the elms.

choices.consequence: You take real pleasure in a girl called Hannah reading a whole page aloud without stumbling. You mean the pleasure. It is not enough and you know it.
You dream three nights running of a red-lit room and wake with your face wet, and you are at the schoolroom door by seven each morning regardless.

nodes.text: St. John comes through the snow at night to tell you a story about a governess who ran from a rich man's house, and then says your real name, which he has read off a scrap of paper you signed and forgot. Your uncle in Madeira has died. Twenty thousand pounds. He mentions, quite evenly, that the man was his uncle also. You have cousins. That is the part you cannot speak for.

choices.consequence: You divide it four ways over his violent objections and take enormous private satisfaction in overruling him. Five thousand is more than you can imagine spending.
You hold the whole sum for a week and discover that being rich alone is exactly as cold as being poor alone, only quieter and better furnished.

nodes.text: He teaches you Hindustani in the evenings and watches you improve at it. Then, on a walk beside a stream, he tells you that God has marked you for the mission field, that you are formed for labour rather than for love, and that you must come with him to India as his wife. He does not pretend to affection. He requires a fellow-soldier. He waits. He is handsome and completely cold.

choices.consequence: You offer to go as his sister and he refuses that flatly, and you understand that he wants the vow precisely because the vow would own you.
For a quarter of an hour you nearly say yes out of sheer hunger to be useful, and you feel that life closing over your head like river water.

nodes.text: His hand is on your head and he is praying and you are very nearly gone. Then, from out past the window and the moor and the whole width of England, you hear your own name said three times in a voice you know. You break away, tell him to leave you, and stand in your dark room asking the night what it wants. Nothing answers. The morning is answer enough.

choices.consequence: You pack at dawn, leave a note for the sisters, and take the coach thirty-six hours east without telling anyone why, because there is no telling it.
You stay one more day and the voice does not come again, which settles it. You go on the Tuesday coach instead of the Monday, and regret the delay.

nodes.text: The innkeeper at Millcote tells it while you hold a cup you do not drink from. Fire in the autumn, set upstairs, the house gutted to the shell. He got every servant out and went back for her, and she stood on the battlements and stepped off. His hand was crushed and taken off at the wrist; one eye may yet be saved. He lives at Ferndean with two old servants and sees nobody.

choices.consequence: You hire a chaise the same afternoon and pay double for the horses, and you send no word ahead, because you want his face before he can arrange it.
You set the cup down and sit an hour deciding whether pity is a reason to spend a life. It is not, and you have five thousand pounds of your own.
You go neither to Ferndean nor to a schoolroom. You buy paper by the quire and begin, on the first page, with a girl behind a curtain in the rain.

nodes.text: You find him at Ferndean feeling for the rain with his one hand. You marry quietly, two witnesses, no veil, no breakfast. Two years on he recovers enough sight in one eye to see that his son has your eyes, and he says so out loud, and then cannot speak for a while. You are together thirty years and you are never once bored. Nobody writes books about a marriage like that. Their loss.

The school takes the five thousand and the better part of a decade. Sixty girls, a stone building with a proper stove, meat twice a week, and not one stool anywhere for standing liars on. You teach Latin, arithmetic, and a thing not on the timetable: that a plain small girl with no money and no family may refuse a wrong life and go and find the right one. Some believe you. A few of them do it.

You publish under a man's name, because a man's name gets the book judged rather than indulged. Most of it happened. The red room happened, and the burnt porridge, and the coach fare that ran out at a crossroads on the moor. Reviewers call it coarse and improper and it sells regardless. In houses you will never enter it stands on the shelf at eye level, its spine gone soft with handling.
